lessons.title: The nutrients animals need
lessons.html:
Why nutrition matters

Feed is usually the biggest cost on a livestock farm. An animal that is fed correctly grows faster, gives more milk, conceives on time and fights disease better. An underfed animal loses condition, stops cycling and becomes sick. To manage feeding well you need to know the main groups of nutrients.

The six nutrient groups

NutrientMain jobExamples of sources
WaterEvery body process; cooling; milkTroughs, dams, boreholes
Energy (carbohydrates and fats)Fuel for movement, warmth, growth and milkMaize, grain, molasses, green grazing
ProteinBuilding muscle, milk, wool, foetusLucerne, oilcake, legumes, urea for ruminants
MineralsBones, teeth, nerves, fertilitySalt, phosphate licks, mineral premix
VitaminsSmall amounts for health and growthGreen feed, sunlight (vitamin D), premix
FibreHealthy rumen and gutHay, veld grass, straw

Water comes first

Animals can survive longer without feed than without water. Clean, cool water must always be available. A lactating cow drinks far more than a dry cow, and all animals drink more in hot weather. Check troughs, ball valves and pipes every day. Dirty or salty water reduces intake and production.

Minerals in South Africa

Many South African veld types are low in phosphorus, especially in summer rainfall areas. Phosphorus shortage causes poor fertility, weak bones and pica, where cattle chew bones and can then get botulism (lamsiekte). This is why phosphate licks are widely used. Salt is also important. Follow the advice of your feed supplier, extension officer or vet for the right lick for your area and season.

lessons.title: How different animals digest feed
lessons.html:
Ruminants and monogastrics

Farm animals digest feed in two main ways. Knowing the difference helps you understand why cattle can live on veld grass while pigs and chickens need concentrated feeds.

Ruminants

Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants. They have a stomach with four parts:

  1. Rumen - a large fermentation vat full of microbes (bacteria and protozoa) that break down fibre.
  2. Reticulum - the honeycomb, which works with the rumen and catches heavy objects like wire and nails.
  3. Omasum - the many-plies, which absorbs water.
  4. Abomasum - the true stomach, which digests with acid and enzymes like our own stomach.

Ruminants chew the cud: they bring feed back up, chew it again and swallow it. A cow that stops chewing the cud is often sick. Because the rumen microbes can use non-protein nitrogen, ruminants can be given urea in licks, but only in correct, small amounts according to the label, because too much urea kills animals quickly.

Monogastrics

Pigs, poultry and people have a simple stomach. They cannot digest much fibre, so they need feeds high in energy and good-quality protein, such as maize and soya meal. Horses are monogastrics with a large hindgut (caecum) that does ferment fibre, so they can eat hay and grass.

Dangers of sudden feed changes

The rumen microbes need time to adjust. If cattle or sheep suddenly eat a lot of grain, the rumen becomes acid (acidosis) and animals can die. Lush legumes such as lucerne can cause bloat. Always change rations slowly over about two to three weeks, and never let hungry animals get into a grain store.

lessons.title: Practical feeding on the farm
lessons.html:
Matching feed to needs

Animals need different amounts of feed at different stages. A ration is the total feed an animal eats in a day. A maintenance ration keeps a dry, non-working animal at the same mass. Extra feed is needed for growth, late pregnancy, milk production and work.

Types of feed

  • Roughage - bulky, high in fibre: veld grass, hay, silage, straw.
  • Concentrates - low in fibre, high in energy or protein: maize, oilcake meal, pellets.
  • Supplements and licks - small amounts to correct a shortage, such as a winter protein lick or a summer phosphate lick.

Seasons on the veld

In summer, sweetveld and sourveld are green and fairly high in protein, but sourveld loses quality quickly as it matures. In winter, dry grass is low in protein, so animals need a protein lick to help the rumen digest the dry grass. In drought, extra roughage may have to be bought in.

Body condition scoring

Body condition score (BCS) is a hands-on way to see if animals are getting enough feed. Feel the ribs, spine and tail-head. On a 1 to 5 scale, 1 is very thin and 5 is very fat. Score regularly and adjust feeding before animals get too thin or too fat.

Good feeding habits

  • Provide enough trough space so shy animals also eat.
  • Keep feed dry; never feed mouldy feed.
  • Store feed safely away from rats and away from chemicals.
  • Weigh or measure feed rather than guessing.
  • Record what was fed and to which group.

Key points

  • The six nutrient groups are water, energy, protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre.
  • Clean water must always be available.
  • Ruminants ferment fibre in the rumen; pigs and poultry need concentrated feed.
  • Change rations slowly to avoid acidosis and bloat.
  • Use body condition scoring and season to adjust feeding.
